title: Cap. XII: Blancus 1648 — Omnes peccaverunt in Adam; Conf. XI denied
pass_a_gloss: You see that this vice is truly sin, that it makes all men guilty of eternal death before God unless it is forgiven—[that it] is imputed—and will you deny that we need the imputation of Christ's merits that we may be justified from this vice? So those who oppose us in this cause are guilty of the very fault of which they falsely accuse us: for they depart from the received doctrine. What he therefore adds—'O how excellent, how wonderful, that whole doctrine of our evangelical justification! from these φρονημάτα it will either wholly collapse, or at least be rendered useless'—you see, I think, Reader, how false and slanderous it is. The same happens to the most distinguished man D. Stephen Blancus, whose Theological Disputation on the origin of the human soul and the mode by which original sin is propagated came to light in the same year 1648. For in Thesis XLII he disputes thus. All sinned by that sin, namely, which entered the world through one man; but they did not sin by that sin in their own person, because they did not yet exist. Therefore they sinned in Adam, inasmuch as in him they died (1 Cor. 15:22). Although the conclusion could be admitted if rightly understood, yet the minor proposition seems to be nothing other than the denial of what is asserted in that article XI by our Churches. For he denies that that vice is the sin which entered the world—that is, into all men—through one man; yet in that article that vice is said both to be truly sin and to make all and every human being guilty of eternal death before God; which it could not effect unless it had entered into all and every human being.
pass_b_english: You see this vice is truly sin, that it makes every man liable to eternal death before God unless it is forgiven—that it is imputed—and will you still deny we need Christ's merits imputed to be justified from it? So our opponents in this cause are guilty of the very charge they falsely lay on us: they leave the received doctrine. When he adds how excellent and wonderful our whole evangelical justification would look—yet from these φρονημάτα it must either fall wholly or at least become useless—you see, Reader, how false and slanderous that is. The same befell the distinguished D. Stephen Blancus, whose Theological Disputation on the soul's origin and how original sin is propagated appeared in 1648. In Thesis XLII he argues: all sinned by the sin that entered the world through one man; yet not in their own person, for they did not yet exist; therefore they sinned in Adam, for in him they died (1 Cor. 15:22). The conclusion could stand if rightly taken; but the minor looks like nothing but a denial of what article XI asserts in our Churches. He denies that the vice is the sin which entered the world—that is, all men—through one man; yet that article says the vice is truly sin and makes every human being liable to eternal death before God, which it could not do unless it had entered every human being.
source_text: Vides hoc vitium esse vere peccatum, omnes homines aeternae mortis reos coram Deo peragere, nisi condonetur, imputari, & negabis nobis opus esse imputatione meritorum Christi ut justificemur ab hoc vitio? Ita qui nobis in hac causa adversantur ejus culpae rei sunt, cujus nos falso accusant: discedunt enim a recepta doctrina. Quod ergo addit, O sic tota illa nostrae justificationis evangelicae doctrina, quam eximia, quam admiranda! ex horum φρονημάτων aut corruet tota, aut saltem inutilis reddetur; cernis, ut opinor, Lector, quam falsum & calumniosum sit. Idem accidit Clarissimo viro D. Steph. Blanco, cujus Disputatio Theologica de animae humanae origine, & modo quo propagatur peccatum originale prodiit in lucem eodem anno 1648. Is enim Th. XLII. sic disputat. Omnes peccaverunt peccato scilicet illo, quod per unum hominem introiit in mundum; at non peccaverunt peccato illo in sua persona, quia non extiterunt. Ergo peccaverunt in Adamo, quippe in quo mortui sunt I. Cor. 15. 22. Quanquam enim admitti posset conclusio, si recte intelligeretur; tamen minor propositio nihil aliud esse videtur, quam eius negatio, quod articulo illo XI. ab Ecclesiis nostris asseritur. Negat enim vitium illud esse peccatum quod per unum hominem in mundum, id est, in omnes homines introiit, quod tamen vitium in illo articulo & vere peccatum esse, & omnes & singulos homines reos mortis aeternae coram Deo peragere dicitur; quod efficere non posset, nisi in omnes & singulos homines introiisset.
